title: Of Course, Kids Are Distracted in Class. But It’s an Easier Fix Than We Think.
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: Katherine Martinko, in a piece first published in the Globe and Mail, argues that Canadian public schools face an attention crisis created by lenient, inconsistent phone policies and an enthusiastic embrace of educational technology. She cites research that students using laptops spend 38 minutes of every hour off task and draws on Jared Cooney-Horvath's claim that Gen Z scores below its parents on literacy, numeracy, creativity and IQ. Her preferred remedy is a strict bell-to-bell phone ban mandated provincially, but she says schools can act now without committees or budgets. She proposes four small changes: stop using QR codes for assignments, keep team and club communication off social media, end device-based games and free time as rewards, and keep earbuds out of class. She admits these will not solve the broader problem of superfluous ed-tech and phones, yet argues they send a clear signal that learning outranks administrative convenience.
points: Martinko frames classroom distraction as the predictable result of loose phone rules combined with heavy ed-tech use, backed by data on off-task laptop time.
A provincial bell-to-bell phone ban, including lunch and recess, is her preferred fix, and she says U.S. schools that adopted one report strong results.
Using QR codes for homework forces students to pull out phones and sends a mixed message about the school's stance on smartphones.
Keeping teams and clubs off Instagram and Snapchat protects families who are trying to delay social media, and plain email or a website serves the same purpose.
Screen-based games and device time as a reward undercut focus, and she cites Prodigy's own figure of 888 questions to raise a test score by one point.
quotes: There is an attention crisis in Canada’s public schools. Thanks to overly lenient and inconsistent phone policies, along with an enthusiastic embrace of educational technology, we have created conditions that make it more difficult than ever for students to focus on learning, which happens to be the point of going to school.

The obvious solution is for all provincial education departments to mandate a strict bell-to-bell phone ban that physically separates students from their devices for the duration of the school day, including lunch and recess.
It may feel convenient for the teacher who saves time and paper, but it’s inconvenient for the student who must fend off (or succumb to) distraction while reading the assignment on their phone.
Instead, teams can use an e-mail newsletter, a Google document, a regularly updated website, a group messaging app that is accessible from a computer or even an old-fashioned bulletin board.
Furthermore, offering screen-based play as a reward can motivate a child to rush through their work in order to get to the device.
These few simple changes won’t solve the broader problem of superfluous EdTech and phones in schools, but they can help reinforce teachers in the continuing battle for students’ attention.
